Why this matters
A Python script that works on one laptop can still fail on another because the second machine has a
different Python version, missing system libraries, different environment variables or an unexpected
filesystem layout. A container gives the program a declared runtime boundary. It does not magically make
bad code reliable, but it reduces the number of hidden machine assumptions you need to remember.
Picture it in your head
Picture shipping a small workshop in a sealed crate. The crate contains the tools and instructions needed by
the worker. The host machine still supplies the ground, electricity and kernel, but the workshop no longer
depends on whatever random tools happen to be lying around the host.
New words before use
image = reusable filesystem/runtime package; container = one running instance of an image; registry =
place that stores/distributes images; host = machine running the container engine; isolation = separate
process/filesystem/network views, not a separate physical computer.
Follow with me once
First compare two runbooks. Runbook A says 'install Python, pip install these things, set these variables,
then hope the path is right.' Runbook B says 'build this Dockerfile, then run this image with this
configuration.' In the supplied Docker lab, the worker has only one job: fetch a CSV from the `source`
service and write a report. The image packages the worker code; the URL and output destination stay
outside the image as configuration.
docker version
docker run --rm hello-world
docker image ls
docker ps -a
What you should see
On a learner PC with Docker working, `hello-world` proves the engine can pull an image and start a
container. `docker image ls` shows stored images; `docker ps -a` shows container instances. These
commands require a working Docker engine on the learner PC. Save their real output there; static course
checks do not substitute for runtime evidence.
Break it / common failure
A common mistake is saying 'the container includes its own operating system.' Linux containers usually
share the host kernel. Another mistake is treating a container as durable storage. If business data exists
only in a disposable writable layer, removing the container can remove that state.
Reason through a realistic incident
A new teammate clones the repository on a clean laptop. The Python script fails outside Docker because
their interpreter and packages differ from yours, but the image build succeeds. That is useful evidence that
the container removed host-runtime assumptions. Now imagine the image still produces a wrong total:
Docker cannot repair transformation logic. Separate environment reproducibility from business correctness
before celebrating the fix.
Why the repair is safe
Containers improve reproducibility only when the build is reproducible, the configuration boundary is
explicit, and persistent state is handled separately. A containerized pipeline can still be non-idempotent,
insecure or logically wrong.
Now you do a changed version alone
Write a before/after environment story for `worker.py`: list what must be installed/configured without
Docker, then list what moves into the image and what deliberately remains runtime configuration. Explain
one problem containers solve and one problem they do not solve.
Fresh changed retry
A colleague says, 'We use Docker, so dependency pinning no longer matters.' Refute the statement using
the difference between an image recipe and an unpinned package install inside that recipe.
Validation and recovery ladder
State the intended partition/grain/side effect before changing code or configuration.
Identify the earliest layer that disagrees with expectation:
build/config/network/schedule/task/data/result.
Inspect the smallest concrete evidence: resolved Compose config, container/task log, input partition,
output file, count or total.
Reveal only the next structural hint. Open the Explained Review only after a saved genuine attempt.
Close review and complete the changed retry. Preserve the failed attempt beside the repair.
Ready-made revision
Containers improve reproducibility only when the build is reproducible, the configuration boundary is
explicit, and persistent state is handled separately. A containerized pipeline can still be non-idempotent,
insecure or logically wrong.
Evidence / mastery
Save your actual command/config/code, observed output/error, one independent validation, a 60-90 second
own-words explanation, and the changed retry. If live Docker/Airflow is required by the lesson, record it as
PENDING until you actually run it on the learner PC - do not convert static evidence into a fake runtime

Why this matters
An image and a container are related but not interchangeable. Confusing them causes learners to delete
the wrong thing, rebuild when they only needed to restart, or assume runtime changes altered the original
image.
Picture it in your head
An image is a cookie cutter plus recipe; a container is one cookie made from it. You can make many
containers from one image. Changing one running container does not silently rewrite the image used to
create the next one.
New words before use
layer = filesystem change in an image build; tag = human-readable image reference; container writable
layer = ephemeral changes made by one container; immutable artifact = build result treated as fixed
rather than edited in place.
Follow with me once
The learner lab builds one `m10-worker:v1` image and can create many short-lived worker containers from
it. The input URL changes through an environment variable. That means the same image can process a
different source without rebuilding. Inspecting image history and container configuration teaches you which
decision belongs at build time versus run time.
docker build -t m10-worker:v1 .
docker image inspect m10-worker:v1
docker run --rm -e SOURCE_URL=http://example.invalid/orders.csv m10-worker:v1
What you should see
The image remains after a short-lived container exits. A failed run caused by a deliberately invalid URL does
not imply the image vanished. Re-running with corrected runtime configuration creates a new container
from the same image.
Break it / common failure
Do not debug every container problem by rebuilding. A wrong environment variable is a runtime-config
problem. Conversely, editing a host source file will not change an already-built image unless that file is
bind-mounted or the image is rebuilt.
Reason through a realistic incident
An engineer shells into a running container, installs a package manually and says the image has been fixed.
Stop and test the claim: create a second container from the same image. The package is absent because
the manual change lived only in the first container writable layer. A durable repair belongs in the
Dockerfile/build inputs, followed by a new image tag and a fresh container.
Why the repair is safe
Promotion usually moves immutable image candidates between environments while environment-specific
configuration changes outside the image. This makes rollback and audit much easier than hand-editing
running machines.
Now you do a changed version alone
Draw an image-to-container one-to-many diagram. For five changes - Python base version, application
source, input URL, host port and API token - classify whether each normally belongs to image build, runtime
configuration or secret management.
Fresh changed retry
Imagine two containers created from the same image produce different output because they were given
different `SOURCE_URL` values. Explain why this does not violate image immutability.

State the intended partition/grain/side effect before changing code or configuration.
Identify the earliest layer that disagrees with expectation:
build/config/network/schedule/task/data/result.
Inspect the smallest concrete evidence: resolved Compose config, container/task log, input partition,
output file, count or total.

Why this matters
A Dockerfile is executable infrastructure documentation: it turns source files and build instructions into an
image. The order of instructions affects cache reuse, attack surface and whether another engineer can
reproduce the same runtime.
Picture it in your head
Picture an assembly line. Each instruction adds a controlled step to the product. If you keep moving the first
workstation, every later station must repeat its work; if stable steps come first, later rebuilds can reuse
them.
New words before use
base image = starting filesystem/runtime; WORKDIR = default working directory; COPY = add build-context
files; RUN = command executed while building; USER = runtime user; CMD = default process; build context
= files Docker may send to the builder.
Follow with me once
Open `practice/docker/Dockerfile`. It starts from `python:3.13-slim`, creates an unprivileged user, copies
only `worker.py`, and runs the worker with exec-form `CMD`. The worker uses only the Python standard
library, so the example avoids fake dependency complexity and lets you focus on the build boundary.
docker build -t m10-worker:v1 practice/docker
docker history m10-worker:v1
docker inspect m10-worker:v1 --format '{{.Config.User}}'
What you should see
The image should build from the documented context and report `appuser` as the runtime user. `docker
history` should show the build steps. The build is not considered proven in this artifact environment
because Docker is absent here; the Dockerfile is statically checked instead.
Break it / common failure
Do not `COPY . .` blindly from a large project that contains `.env`, virtual environments or evidence files.
Do not put passwords in `ENV` or `RUN` instructions; image history and layers can preserve them. Do not
use root merely because it avoids permissions learning.
Reason through a realistic incident
A Dockerfile works but rebuilds slowly and accidentally includes a local `.env`. Inspect build context and
instruction order. The correct repair is not 'use more CPU'; exclude unnecessary/sensitive files, copy stable
dependency metadata before frequently changing source, and rebuild. Then inspect image history/config
rather than assuming the secret disappeared because the final app starts normally.
Why the repair is safe
A professional Dockerfile makes the runtime boundary reviewable: known base, minimal context,
deterministic dependency install, explicit work directory, non-root user and a clear foreground process.
Now you do a changed version alone
Explain every instruction in the supplied Dockerfile in one sentence. Then modify a working copy so
`worker.py` is copied to `/opt/m10/worker.py`; update WORKDIR/CMD consistently and predict what breaks
if only one path is changed.
Fresh changed retry
Add a requirements file containing one package. Reorder the Dockerfile so dependency metadata is
copied/installed before frequently changing application source. Explain the cache benefit without claiming
the cache proves packages are pinned.
Validation and recovery ladder
State the intended partition/grain/side effect before changing code or configuration.
Identify the earliest layer that disagrees with expectation:
build/config/network/schedule/task/data/result.
Inspect the smallest concrete evidence: resolved Compose config, container/task log, input partition,
output file, count or total.
Reveal only the next structural hint. Open the Explained Review only after a saved genuine attempt.
Close review and complete the changed retry. Preserve the failed attempt beside the repair.

deterministic dependency install, explicit work directory, non-root user and a clear foreground process.

Why this matters
A service listening inside a container is not automatically reachable from the host. Port publishing is an
explicit network boundary. The most common beginner error is mixing up the host port with the port where
the process listens inside the container.
Picture it in your head
Picture an apartment building. The container process listens at an apartment door (container port). Port
publishing creates a reception-desk rule that forwards one building entrance number (host port) to that
apartment door.
New words before use
container port = where the process listens inside container namespace; host/published port = host-side
entry point; EXPOSE = image metadata/documentation, not automatic publication; localhost = the current
network namespace, not a universal name for 'my laptop'.
Follow with me once
The supplied Compose lab publishes the source service as `${SOURCE_PORT:-8090}:8000`. From the host
you can request `http://localhost:8090/orders.csv`. From the worker container you must use
`http://source:8000/orders.csv`. The two addresses reach the same service from different network
locations.
docker compose up -d source
docker compose ps
# host: http://localhost:8090/orders.csv
# worker network: http://source:8000/orders.csv
What you should see
`docker compose ps` should show a host mapping similar to `0.0.0.0:8090->8000/tcp`. Changing
`SOURCE_PORT` changes only the host entry point; the service-to-service port remains 8000.
Break it / common failure
`EXPOSE 8000` does not publish port 8000. Publishing `8090:8000` also does not make the source process
listen on 8090 inside the container. If a process listens only on 127.0.0.1 inside some container scenarios,
publication may still not behave as you expect; always inspect the actual bind/listen configuration.
Reason through a realistic incident
The source service is healthy inside its container, but `http://localhost:8000` on the host fails while `docker
compose ps` shows `8090->8000`. The evidence says the host must call port 8090. If the worker calls the
source from the Compose network, it uses `source:8000`. One service therefore has two correct addresses
depending on the caller's network namespace.
Why the repair is safe
Expose only interfaces that need host/external access. Databases and internal services often communicate
on private container networks without publishing every port to the host.
Now you do a changed version alone
Change the host port to 8095 without changing the container port. State the host URL and the worker's
internal URL. Explain why the worker should not start calling `localhost:8095`.
Fresh changed retry
Port 8090 is already occupied on your laptop. Design the smallest safe correction and explain why
rebuilding the image would be unrelated to the conflict.

Identify the earliest layer that disagrees with expectation:
build/config/network/schedule/task/data/result.
Inspect the smallest concrete evidence: resolved Compose config, container/task log, input partition,
output file, count or total.
Reveal only the next structural hint. Open the Explained Review only after a saved genuine attempt.
Close review and complete the changed retry. Preserve the failed attempt beside the repair.

on private container networks without publishing every port to the host.

Why this matters
Containers are replaceable processes. Business state should not depend on one container's writable layer
surviving forever. Volumes and bind mounts deliberately separate persistent or shared data from the
container lifecycle.
Picture it in your head
Imagine replacing a rented office every day. If the ledger is taped to the office wall, replacement loses it. A
named storage locker survives office replacement. A bind mount is more like giving the office direct access
to a specific host folder.
New words before use
named volume = Docker-managed persistent storage; bind mount = host path mounted into a container;
writable layer = container-local ephemeral filesystem changes; read-only mount = mounted content the
container may read but not modify.
Follow with me once
In `compose.yaml`, the source CSV folder is bind-mounted read-only because it is learner-controlled input.
The worker writes its report into the named `report_data` volume. `docker compose down` removes
containers but keeps the named volume; `docker compose down -v` intentionally deletes it.
docker compose up --build
docker volume ls
docker compose down
docker compose up --build
# deliberate reset only:
docker compose down -v
What you should see
After ordinary `down` and `up`, the named volume still exists. After `down -v`, it is removed. The source
bind mount remains on the host because it was never Docker-managed volume data.
Break it / common failure
Never teach `docker compose down -v` as routine cleanup when the volume contains data you care about.
Also avoid bind-mounting broad host folders with write access just to bypass permissions. Mount only what
the service needs.
Reason through a realistic incident
A learner runs `docker compose down -v` to 'clean up' and loses a database volume. Recreate the timeline:
`down` removes service containers/network but normally leaves named volumes; `down -v` explicitly
removes project volumes. The recovery lesson is operational, not syntactic: destructive cleanup flags
belong in documented reset procedures, and important volume data still needs backups.
Why the repair is safe
State ownership is an architectural decision. Volumes survive container replacement but do not by
themselves provide backup, replication, retention or corruption recovery.
Now you do a changed version alone
Classify five paths - immutable input CSV, generated report, application source during development,
database data directory, secret file - as image content, bind mount, named volume or secret mechanism.
Defend each choice.
Fresh changed retry
A teammate says 'the database is in a container, so backups are unnecessary because the volume
persists.' Explain why persistence and backup/recovery are different controls.

build/config/network/schedule/task/data/result.

output file, count or total.

Close review and complete the changed retry. Preserve the failed attempt beside the repair.

Why this matters
Multi-container systems fail surprisingly often because one service calls `localhost` when it really needs
another service. Compose gives services a shared default network and DNS-based service discovery so
code can use stable service names instead of container IP addresses.
Picture it in your head
Inside each container, `localhost` means 'this room'. Calling another service is like calling another room by
its directory name. Compose supplies the directory; hard-coded IP addresses are like memorizing a hotel
room number that can change after checkout.
New words before use
service name = Compose DNS name; default network = automatically created Compose network; bridge
network = common local Docker network driver; DNS/service discovery = name-to-address resolution
inside the network.
Follow with me once
The worker uses `SOURCE_URL=http://source:8000/orders.csv`. `source` is the Compose service name. No
container IP appears in the code. Bring the source service down and the worker loses the dependency;
bring it back and the same name resolves to the replacement container.
docker compose up -d source
docker compose run --rm worker
docker compose exec source hostname
docker network ls
What you should see
With both services on the same Compose network, the worker can resolve `source`. The host-facing URL
still uses localhost and the published port. The internal URL uses service name plus container port.
Break it / common failure
Do not fix a service-to-service failure by copying the current container IP into source code. Do not assume
`depends_on` means the dependency is ready to serve; start order and readiness are different concepts. A
health check or application retry may still be necessary.
Reason through a realistic incident
The worker suddenly cannot reach `source` after someone changed the Compose service name to `feed`.
A copied container IP works briefly, then fails after recreation. The durable repair is to update the
service-name configuration and keep name-based discovery. This incident demonstrates why ephemeral
addresses are runtime details and why configuration should refer to stable service identities.
Why the repair is safe
Stable service discovery plus health/readiness checks is safer than coding around ephemeral addresses.
Network boundaries also help you avoid publishing internal-only services to the host.
Now you do a changed version alone
Explain three addresses: `localhost:8090` from the host, `source:8000` from worker, and `localhost:8000`
from inside source. State which namespace each `localhost` refers to.
Fresh changed retry
Rename the Compose service from `source` to `feed`. List every configuration reference that should
change and every place that should not need an IP update.

Identify the earliest layer that disagrees with expectation:
build/config/network/schedule/task/data/result.
Inspect the smallest concrete evidence: resolved Compose config, container/task log, input partition,
output file, count or total.
Reveal only the next structural hint. Open the Explained Review only after a saved genuine attempt.
Close review and complete the changed retry. Preserve the failed attempt beside the repair.

Network boundaries also help you avoid publishing internal-only services to the host.

Why this matters
Compose turns a collection of container commands into a version-controlled application definition. But a
reproducible stack still needs disciplined configuration and secret boundaries; putting every value into
YAML is not the same as managing it well.
Picture it in your head
Think of Compose as a stage manager's cue sheet: which actors exist, which props/volumes they use,
which doors/ports open, what environment cues they receive and which actor must be healthy before
another starts.
New words before use
service = one application component; compose.yaml = multi-service definition; interpolation = substituting
environment values into config; secret = sensitive value needing restricted handling; health check =
command that reports service readiness/health.
Follow with me once
Read `compose.yaml` with `docker compose config` before running it. The file defines source and worker
services, a published source port, a read-only input bind mount, a persistent report volume and a source
health check. `.env.example` documents safe non-secret values. The project intentionally contains no real
credentials.
cd practice/docker
cp .env.example .env
docker compose config
docker compose up --build
docker compose logs
docker compose down
What you should see
`docker compose config` should resolve variables and show service/network/volume structure before any
container starts. The worker should eventually write one report based on the served CSV. A clean clone
should need only documented environment values, not hidden machine state.
Break it / common failure
Never commit real passwords merely because they are in `.env`. `.env` is configuration storage, not
automatically a secret vault. Do not use Compose Variables as a substitute for production secret backends.
Also do not call `down -v` casually.
Reason through a realistic incident
A stack works only on the original developer laptop because they relied on an untracked `.env` and an
already-existing named volume. A second learner gets a different port and empty output. Reproducibility
means documenting required non-secret config, validating the resolved Compose file with `docker compose
config`, and distinguishing intentional persistent state from hidden stale state.
Why the repair is safe
Version-control safe structure and names; inject environment-owned values at runtime; store real secrets in
a secrets mechanism appropriate to the deployment environment. Reproducibility means a clean
environment can rebuild the same topology from documented inputs.
Now you do a changed version alone
From a blank page, reconstruct a two-service Compose design: source + worker, internal service-name
URL, one host port, read-only input and named output volume. Then compare to the supplied file and
record only differences that matter.
Fresh changed retry
Move the host port and output volume name through environment interpolation. Explain why changing
those values should not require rebuilding the worker image.

build/config/network/schedule/task/data/result.
Inspect the smallest concrete evidence: resolved Compose config, container/task log, input partition,
output file, count or total.
Reveal only the next structural hint. Open the Explained Review only after a saved genuine attempt.
Close review and complete the changed retry. Preserve the failed attempt beside the repair.

Why this matters
A cron line can start a script, but production workflows need more than start time: dependency order,
retries, run history, backfill semantics, parameterization, observability and safe recovery. Orchestration is
the control plane that coordinates work; it should not hide the business transformation logic.
Picture it in your head
Picture an airport control tower. The tower does not fly the planes or load the luggage; it coordinates when
each movement is allowed, watches state, handles delays and keeps a history of what happened.
New words before use
orchestration = coordinating tasks/runs/dependencies; workflow = connected units of work; run = one
execution instance; control plane = system coordinating work; idempotent = repeatable without
multiplying logical state.
Follow with me once
Run `practice/simulator/scripts/orchestration_simulator.py` before touching Airflow. It processes
date-partitioned order files, writes one deterministic report per partition, records attempts and can rerun a
partition safely. This separates the workflow concept from one orchestration vendor.
python practice/simulator/scripts/orchestration_simulator.py \
--input-dir practice/simulator/input --output-dir practice/simulator/output
ic
Three partitions should produce row counts 4, 3 and 5. Re-running should overwrite the same partition
result with the same business totals rather than append duplicate logical output. That behavior is what
later makes backfill/retry discussion concrete.
Break it / common failure
Do not move all transformation code into a huge DAG file just because Airflow can run Python. Do not make
orchestration responsible for fixing bad source semantics. Keep the business work testable outside the
scheduler where possible.
Reason through a realistic incident
A nightly script is launched by cron and sometimes starts before its source file exists. The team adds
`sleep(900)` and now every run waits even when data arrives early. An orchestrator lets you model the

Why this matters

readiness. A sensor models waiting as a first-class task, but inefficient waiting can occupy resources for
hours.
Picture it in your head
A sensor is a guard at a gate. The guard should check whether the delivery arrived, then step aside
efficiently between checks rather than occupying the loading dock doing nothing.
New words before use
sensor = task that waits for condition; poke interval = how often condition is checked; timeout = maximum
total wait; deferrable = waiting mode that frees a worker slot where supported; file sensor = waits for
file/path condition.
Follow with me once
The supplied Airflow scaffold includes a separate `m10_wait_for_file.py` example using the standard
provider FileSensor with a bounded timeout and deferrable mode. The main daily Dag can stay runnable
without depending on that example. The point is to understand resource-safe waiting, not to add sensors
everywhere.
FileSensor(
task_id='wait_for_partition',
filepath='/data/orders_2026-09-03.csv',
poke_interval=60, timeout=1800, deferrable=True,
What you should see
A sensor succeeds only when its condition is true; it should fail after the declared timeout rather than wait
forever. Deferrable support depends on the provider/runtime and must be proven in the learner
environment.
Break it / common failure
Do not write `while True: sleep(...)` inside an ordinary worker task as your default waiting strategy. Do not
use a 1-second poke interval for a file expected once per hour. Do not omit timeout and create endless
invisible waiting.
Reason through a realistic incident
A file sensor checks every second for a partner file that normally arrives once per hour. Hundreds of
unnecessary checks consume resources and clutter logs. Increase the poke interval, keep a meaningful
timeout and use deferrable waiting when supported. Reliability includes the cost of waiting, not just
whether the condition eventually becomes true.
Why the repair is safe
Waiting is capacity planning. A correct sensor defines condition, cadence, timeout, resource mode and
failure ownership; otherwise a quiet wait can be as operationally expensive as a failed task.
Now you do a changed version alone
Choose sensible poke interval and timeout for three cases: file expected within 5 minutes, partner file
within 2 hours, daily data warehouse table expected by 08:00. Defend resource vs detection-latency
tradeoffs.
Fresh changed retry
The external platform can emit an event instead of being polled. Explain why event-driven/deferrable
waiting may be better than frequent polling and what failure/timeout behavior still needs definition.

Why this matters
Logs are evidence, not decoration. When a workflow fails, you need to reconstruct which run, task,
partition, attempt and input caused the failure without leaking sensitive data into the log stream.
Picture it in your head
Think of a flight recorder: useful events have identity and sequence. 'Something failed' is not enough; a
useful record says which run, what input boundary, what check failed and what recovery was attempted.
New words before use
structured context = consistent identifiers/fields in logs; attempt = retry number; traceback = exception
call path; import error = Dag parse/load problem; task log = runtime evidence for one task instance.
Follow with me once
The simulator writes run summaries containing partition, row count, total, attempt and status. The Airflow
task examples use Python logging and include partition/run context without printing secrets. For a missing
Dag, check import errors; for a failed task, open that task instance log; for wrong data with green tasks,
inspect validation controls rather than assuming orchestration success equals correctness.
logger.info('partition=%s rows=%s total=%s', partition, rows, total)
# never: logger.info('password=%s', password)
What you should see
A failure can be traced to a specific partition/attempt and compared with a later repaired attempt. The logs
contain enough context to reproduce the problem but no password/token literals.
Break it / common failure
Do not log entire dataframes or response bodies containing PII/secrets merely because debugging is hard.
Do not erase failed logs/evidence after repair. Do not read only the final exception line when the earlier
stack/context shows the actual cause.
Reason through a realistic incident
A publish task fails after three retries. The final log line says only 'ValueError', but the earlier context line
identifies partition `2026-09-03`, row count 5 and one duplicate key. The fastest recovery comes from
structured context plus the traceback. If logs had printed a real token during debugging, that token would
now need rotation even though the task failure was unrelated.
Why the repair is safe
Operationally useful logging connects workflow state to data evidence. Preserve failed attempts, sanitize
sensitive values, and design logs so another engineer can diagnose without reproducing your entire local
setup.

Why this matters
Catchup and backfill are where sloppy date logic becomes expensive. Historical processing must target
historical partitions, avoid duplicate side effects and preserve normal current state. Reprocessing should be
an explicit operation, not 'change the computer clock and rerun.'
Picture it in your head
Imagine filling missing pages in a ledger. Each historical page has its own date label. You can fill pages 3
through 7 later, but you must write into those pages - not today's page five times.
New words before use
catchup = scheduler creates missed historical intervals from start boundary; backfill = intentionally run a
historical range; reprocessing = rerun prior work; idempotent sink = repeated run converges to same
logical state.
Follow with me once
Use the simulator with Sep 1-3, then delete only the Sep 2 output and rerun Sep 2. The partition total
should return to the same value. Next run all three again and prove totals do not multiply. In Airflow, derive
paths from data interval, not wall-clock time.
python practice/simulator/scripts/orchestration_simulator.py \
--input-dir practice/simulator/input --output-dir practice/simulator/output
ic
Each date has one deterministic output file. Reprocessing Sep 2 replaces/converges that partition rather
than appending a second logical copy. A historical range can be reasoned about before using Airflow's live
backfill commands.
Break it / common failure
Do not backfill a non-idempotent external write without duplicate/transaction controls. Do not let historical
runs overwrite a shared `latest.csv`. Do not assume `catchup=True` is always desirable; choose based on
whether missed historical intervals should run.
Reason through a realistic incident
A backfill of seven days writes every run to `output/latest.json`. All seven runs succeed, but only the final
file survives. The scheduler is green and the data history is destroyed. Partitioned output paths or
idempotent upsert keys are therefore part of orchestration correctness. Historical run identity must survive
into the side effect.
Why the repair is safe
Historical recovery is a first-class reliability feature. Partition identity, side-effect idempotency and explicit
range controls determine whether backfill restores trust or creates duplicate damage.

Why this matters
The final M10 lesson combines container reproducibility with orchestration correctness. A production-style
workflow is not 'Docker works' plus 'DAG is green'; it is a reproducible runtime whose historical runs,
retries, configuration, side effects, evidence and recovery all agree with the data contract.
Picture it in your head
Picture a factory line inside a well-labeled portable building. Docker controls the repeatable
building/runtime. Airflow controls when each station is allowed to work. Data-quality controls decide
whether the product is acceptable. Logs and saved evidence let another operator explain and recover the
line.
New words before use
reproducible environment = same declared build/topology from clean state; orchestration invariant =
condition that must remain true across runs/retries; operational handoff = enough
code/config/runbook/evidence for another engineer to operate safely.
Follow with me once
Complete two proofs. First, inspect the Docker project from a clean configuration: image recipe,
service-name network boundary, output volume and no secret literals. Second, run the pure-Python
orchestration simulator across Sep 1-3 including a one-time transient failure and a safe rerun. Then
statically inspect the Airflow 3.3.1 Dag for `airflow.sdk`, interval-derived partitions, bounded retries,
Params and small task communication.
python practice/run_static_qa.py
python practice/simulator/scripts/orchestration_simulator.py \
--input-dir practice/simulator/input --output-dir practice/simulator/output
ic
Static/local QA proves the files are internally coherent and the simulator demonstrates deterministic
partition behavior. It does NOT prove Docker Engine, Airflow scheduler/UI or DagRun behavior on the

Break it / common failure
Do not use a passing static parser as evidence that Docker networking works. Do not use a green Airflow

The final pipeline passes static checks and the simulator, but Docker Desktop has never been started and
the Airflow Dag has never parsed on the learner PC. The correct status is not 'production ready'; it is
'static/local logic validated, native runtime pending'. After real runtime proof, keep the same discipline:
Docker success, Airflow success and data reconciliation are three separate claims that all need evidence.
